nameStory: The horizontal pelt lichen gets its name from its flat, sprawling growth pattern that lies horizontally across the ground like an animal pelt spread out to dry. The "pelt" part comes from its leather-like texture and earthy colors that resemble tanned animal hide. This lichen truly does look like nature's own furry carpet laid flat against the forest floor.
description: Horizontal pelt lichen is a large, leafy lichen that forms broad, flat patches on soil and moss in shaded forests. It has a distinctive leather-like texture with lobed edges that spread horizontally across the ground, rarely curling upward. The upper surface is typically gray-green to brownish, while the underside is pale with prominent dark veins. Individual patches can grow quite large, sometimes reaching several inches across as they slowly expand over many years.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms large, flat, leafy patches that lie completely horizontal against the ground - never curling up at the edges like many other pelt lichens

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels like soft, supple leather when dry, becoming more pliable and slightly spongy when moist

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Upper surface ranges from gray-green to brownish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet

idTips.label: Underside
idTips.description: Pale whitish to cream-colored underneath with distinct dark brown to black branching veins running through it

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on soil, moss, or decaying organic matter on the forest floor, never on tree bark or rocks

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes can span 2-6 inches across, often forming larger colonies that cover significant patches of ground

habitat: Look for horizontal pelt lichen in moist, shaded deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with rich, humus-filled soil. It thrives in cool, humid spots under dense tree canopies where it can grow undisturbed on the forest floor among mosses and leaf litter. You're most likely to find it in mature forests with consistent moisture and protection from direct sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant and noticeable as spring moisture returns, with the upper surface showing its brightest green colors when wet from rain and snowmelt.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more grayish during dry periods, but remains visible and identifiable. Look for it in consistently moist forest spots that stay cool.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as falling leaves reveal patches on the forest floor, and autumn rains bring back the vibrant green coloration.
seasonality.winter: Remains present under snow cover and can be found during winter thaws, appearing quite dark and leathery against the brown forest floor.

funFact: This ancient lichen can live for decades or even centuries, growing so slowly that a patch the size of your hand might be older than you are - some large specimens could have been quietly carpeting the same forest spot since before the American Revolution!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with dog pelt lichen, but remember that horizontal pelt lichen lives up to its name by staying completely flat against the ground, while dog pelt lichen often has edges that curl upward like a dog's ears. Think "horizontal = flat as a pancake" versus "dog ears = curled up."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "pelt" lichen, this species was actually one of the first lichens ever scientifically described, way back in 1762 by British botanist William Hudson. The pelt lichens get their common name from early naturalists who thought these leathery, ground-hugging lichens looked remarkably similar to animal pelts laid out for tanning.
compareHints: Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen. Unlike the fan-shaped fan pelt lichen or the distinctly scaly scaly pelt lichen, horizontal pelt has smooth-edged lobes that spread evenly in all directions. The key is in the name: if it's lying perfectly flat like a rug, you've likely found horizontal pelt lichen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
